_comment: THE VERDICTS THE THREE PORTS OF ONE RULE MUST AGREE ON.
The rule is 'a base URL it is safe to attach a Talyvor API key to'. It is implemented THREE TIMES:
agent/internal/safeurl/safeurl.go (the CLI, returns an error),
extension/src/safeurl-pure.ts (the VS Code extension, returns "" for unsafe), and
jetbrains/src/main/kotlin/com/talyvor/code/SafeUrlPure.kt (the JetBrains plugin, also "").
Measured 2026-08-19 before this file existed: the FIRST TWO disagreed on 6 of the 29 cases
below, in BOTH directions, and the extension's half had ZERO tests of any kind.
THIS HEADER SAID 'TWICE' UNTIL THE THIRD PORT WAS MEASURED, later the same day. It shipped as
a PRIVATE helper inside the JetBrains plugin's TalyvorSettings, so it had no filename of its
own for a census to grep for, and it disagreed with this table on 8 of the 29 cases — SEVEN OF
THEM FAIL-OPEN: https://0xa9fea9fe/ and https://2852039166/ (both 169.254.169.254 respelled),
https://[::]/, and every IPv6 link-local host, each ACCEPTED with the API key attached.
The disagreements were not typos. Each side inherited a different host-normalisation:
Go's url.Hostname() STRIPS the IPv6 brackets and does not normalise legacy IPv4 spellings;
Node's URL.hostname KEEPS the brackets and DOES normalise them; java.net.URI.getHost() KEEPS
the brackets and normalises NOTHING. All three rules were then written as string comparisons
against the shape the author's own runtime produces.
agent/internal/safeurl/cases_parity_test.go, extension/src/safeurl-pure.test.ts and
jetbrains/src/test/kotlin/com/talyvor/code/SafeUrlParityTest.kt each assert their own port
against this file. Fixing one side alone now fails that side; editing this file alone fails
all three. A case here is not a permission — it is a record of a verdict the three guards
must reach TOGETHER.
WARNING TO THE FOURTH PORT: 'editing this file alone fails all three' is true only because
each build DECLARES THIS FILE AN INPUT. Measured: it sits outside the Gradle project, nothing
declared it, and truncating this table from 29 cases to 5 left '> Task :test UP-TO-DATE' —
exit 0, BUILD SUCCESSFUL, zero tests executed, the parity guard's own floor never reached.
(FROM-CACHE is the same hole's other spelling; gradle.properties sets org.gradle.caching=true.)
jetbrains/build.gradle.kts declares it now. A consumer that does not is not a consumer; it is
a copy that happens to agree today.

cases.why: the ordinary case: https to a named host
port and base path are not the guard's business
https to a named host
a DNS label may START with a digit — the numeric-host rule must not eat it
hex-looking DNS label, not a numeric host
https to a LAN IP is the self-host case; only cleartext and link-local are refused
local dev over http is the documented exception
local dev over http

IPv6 loopback IS local dev. The extension refused this: host === '::1' can never be true because Node's URL.hostname keeps the brackets ('[::1]'). Go's url.Hostname() strips them, so the identical line worked there
IPv6 loopback over https
the API key would cross the network in cleartext
a LAN address is still cleartext
resolves to loopback but is not spelled as loopback; the rule is textual on purpose
neither http nor https
no host
does not parse as an absolute URL
cloud metadata service over cleartext
https does NOT make the metadata address safe — this is the case the whole link-local branch exists for
trailing dot. Go kept it, so net.ParseIP returned nil and the link-local branch never ran

169.254.169.254 respelled in hex. MEASURED: the OS resolver returns 169.254.169.254 for it, and Go's own http.Client connects to a loopback listener via 0x7f000001. Go accepted it because net.ParseIP is nil for inet_aton forms
the same address as a single decimal. MEASURED: resolves to 169.254.169.254
octal-leading form. Node normalised it to 127.0.0.1 and the extension accepted it; Go did not normalise and accepted it too, for the opposite reason
short form. Node normalises to 127.0.0.1, Go does not — a host that means different things to the two ports is refused by both
numeric-looking and not an address
unspecified address
IPv6 unspecified. The extension's check was startsWith('[fe80'), which this does not match
IPv6 link-local unicast — the only link-local case the extension's literal prefix caught
fe80::/10 runs to febf, so this IS link-local unicast and the '[fe80' prefix missed it
IPv6 link-local multicast, missed by the same prefix
